chapter_summary:
With navigation, selection, and transformation under your belt, you're now ready to bring new elements into your 3D world! The foundation of almost any 3D model, especially in game development, starts with simple geometric shapes known as **primitives**. These are your building blocks – cubes, spheres, cylinders, planes, and more. Blender provides an easy way to add these to your scene, giving you the raw material to sculpt, extrude, and refine into complex assets.

To add a new object, you'll primarily use the **Add menu**. You can access this in two main ways:
1.  Go to the top menu bar: `Add > Mesh > [Choose your primitive]`.
2.  Use the universal hotkey: **Shift + A**. This brings up a radial menu right under your mouse cursor, making it very fast to add objects.

When you add a new mesh primitive (e.g., `Shift + A > Mesh > Cube`), it will always appear at the location of your **3D Cursor**. This is why understanding the 3D Cursor from the previous chapter is so important! If your 3D Cursor is at the world origin (0,0,0), your new object will appear there. If you've moved the 3D Cursor, the object will appear at that new location. This allows for precise placement right from the start, which is crucial when blocking out game levels or placing specific assets.

Immediately after adding an object, you'll notice a small panel appear in the bottom-left corner of the 3D Viewport, often called the **"Adjust Last Operation"** panel or "redo panel." This panel is incredibly powerful but also temporary – it disappears as soon as you perform another action (like moving the object, selecting something else, or even just clicking away). It allows you to modify the properties of the newly created primitive *before* it's finalized. For example, when adding a UV Sphere, this panel lets you adjust the number of segments and rings, which directly impacts the polygon count and smoothness of the sphere. For game development, controlling polygon count from the very beginning is crucial for performance optimization, as high-poly models can significantly impact frame rates. A common mistake is to ignore this panel, then realize later that the primitive wasn't created with the desired resolution, requiring a rebuild or more complex mesh editing. Always check this panel immediately after adding a primitive!

Once you have objects in your scene, you'll inevitably need to **delete** them. Deleting an object is straightforward:
1.  **Select the object(s)** you wish to delete.
2.  Press the **Delete key** on your keyboard (or `X`).
3.  A confirmation prompt will appear asking "Erase Selected?" Click "Delete" or press `Enter` to confirm.

It's good practice to confirm deletions, especially in complex scenes, to avoid accidentally removing important assets. Safety note: always save your work frequently (`Ctrl+S` or `File > Save`) before performing major deletions or operations, just in case you need to revert to an earlier state. This is a golden rule in any 3D workflow.

Speaking of reverting, **Undo** and **Redo** are your best friends in any creative software, and Blender is no exception.
*   To **Undo** your last action, press **Ctrl + Z**. You can repeatedly press `Ctrl+Z` to undo multiple steps back in your history.
*   To **Redo** an action you just undid, press **Shift + Ctrl + Z`.
Blender keeps a history of your actions, which can be configured in `Edit > Preferences > System > Undo Steps`. A higher number allows you to undo further back, but uses more memory. Always make sure you have enough undo steps to feel comfortable experimenting and correcting mistakes without fear!

As your scenes grow, especially in game development where you might have hundreds or thousands of assets, **scene organization** becomes paramount. Blender uses **Collections** to group objects, similar to layers or folders in other software.
*   You can see your collections in the **Outliner** panel (usually top-right of the default layout).
*   To create a new collection, right-click in the Outliner and choose `New Collection`.
*   To move an object to a collection, select the object, press `M`, and choose an existing collection or `New Collection`.
*   Collections allow you to hide, show, or disable rendering for entire groups of objects, making it much easier to manage complex scenes. For example, you might have a "Characters" collection, an "Environment_Props" collection, and a "Lights" collection. This keeps your workspace clean and efficient, which is crucial when collaborating on larger game projects, allowing team members to focus on specific parts of the scene without interference.

By understanding how to create, delete, and organize basic primitives, you're building a solid foundation for all your future 3D modeling endeavors. These simple shapes, combined with the navigation and transformation skills you've learned, are the starting point for every intricate model you'll ever create, whether it's a simple prop or a complex character for a game.

screens.title: Creating and Deleting Basic Primitives
screens.subtitle: Bring basic geometry into your scene, tweak it immediately, and keep your project tidy.

narration.text: In this chapter you'll learn how to bring the most important building blocks of 3D modeling into your Blender scene, and how to manage them safely. Primitives — cubes, spheres, cylinders, planes and more — are the raw shapes you use to block out props, environments, and characters. You will learn the two main ways to add them, how the 3D Cursor determines where they appear, and how the temporary Adjust Last Operation panel lets you set parameters like sphere segments or cylinder vertices right after creation. We'll also cover the safe ways to delete objects and how Undo and Redo let you recover from or reapply changes. Finally, you'll practice simple scene organization using Collections and the Outliner so that as your scene grows you can hide, isolate, or disable groups of objects quickly. By the end of the lesson you will be able to add a primitive, change its initial properties without redoing work, undo mistakes, and group objects into collections for efficient scene management. Think of these skills as the fundamental cheatsheet you’ll use every time you start a new model or layout a level.

screens.title: Primitives — what they are and why they matter
screens.subtitle: Definition, examples, and how primitives form the basis of modeling

narration.text: Primitives are the basic geometric shapes used as starting points for 3D modeling. Think of them as clay blocks — cubes, UV spheres, icospheres, cylinders, cones, torii, and planes that you place into the scene to block out size, silhouette, and composition. A clear definition helps: a primitive is a mesh generated with a predictable topology and initial parameter set, such as segment counts for a sphere or vertex counts for a cylinder. For example, a UV Sphere created with 32 segments will be much smoother than one with 16 segments; that smoothness also increases polygon count, which matters for game performance. A common misconception is to treat primitives as final models; instead, they are scaffolding. You often adjust them, combine them, and edit them at the vertex level. Practically, start with a low-resolution primitive when blocking or targeting a low-poly game asset, and only increase resolution when a model needs smoothness. Closing takeaway: view primitives as inexpensive shapes to iterate quickly — how might you use a cylinder and a plane together to block a simple prop? Primitives — what they are and why they matter means use low-res primitives to block forms, then refine; they determine initial topology and polygon budget.. In practical terms, definition, examples, and how primitives form the basis of modeling. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Add menu and Shift+A — fast ways to create geometry
screens.subtitle: Two primary methods to add primitives and when to use them

narration.text: There are two primary ways to add primitives in Blender: the Add menu in the top bar and the universal hotkey Shift+A. The top menu is explicit and discoverable: Add > Mesh > choose the primitive. Shift+A brings a radial menu under your cursor, making it quick to add objects without moving your hand away from the viewport. Use Shift+A for fast blocking and the Add menu when you need to navigate nested entries deliberately. When you add a mesh it spawns at the 3D Cursor location, so the cursor’s position determines where geometry appears. For example, if you're blocking a level and want a prop precisely at a doorway, move the 3D Cursor to the doorway and then use Shift+A to place the object exactly where you need it. A common misconception is that new objects always spawn at the world origin; they spawn at the 3D Cursor. Closing takeaway: practice using both Add and Shift+A during a quick blocking session and notice how much faster Shift+A feels when you keep the cursor near your work area. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: 3D Cursor — the spawn point for new objects
screens.subtitle: How cursor placement determines object location and why precise placement matters

narration.text: The 3D Cursor is a simple but crucial tool: it sets where newly added primitives appear. When you add an object using Add > Mesh or Shift+A, the object spawns at the cursor instead of always at the world origin. This allows precise placement when blocking scenes or placing assets during level design. For example, if you move the 3D Cursor to the center of a room, then add a UV Sphere, the sphere will appear exactly at that center without extra translation. A common misconception is thinking the cursor is only for advanced operations — in practice it's a primary placement control. Another important point is that the Adjust Last Operation panel still affects the newly created mesh regardless of cursor position. Closing takeaway: practice moving the 3D Cursor to several locations and adding objects so you feel how it speeds up placement. Ask yourself: how often could placing the cursor first save you a translate step in your modeling workflow? 3D Cursor — the spawn point for new objects means move the 3d cursor to the desired spawn point before adding primitives so objects appear where you want them.. Definition › 3D Cursor
What the 3D Cursor does
It defines spawn location for newly added objects, enabling precise placement without extra translation steps.
Practical tip
Move the cursor before adding to place an object exactly where you need it for blocking or alignment.
Example
Set cursor at the center of a doorway, then add a cylinder to place a column without manual movement.
Key Takeaway

Using the 3D Cursor for precise spawn placement removes redundant transforms and speeds up blocking tasks.

Common misconception
New objects always appear at origin. In fact, they spawn at the 3D Cursor, which may be anywhere in the scene.
Check your understanding

screens.title: Adjust Last Operation panel — tweak parameters immediately
screens.subtitle: Use the temporary redo panel to change segments, rings, vertices and sizes

narration.text: The Adjust Last Operation panel appears in the bottom-left of the 3D Viewport immediately after you add a primitive. It’s temporary: as soon as you perform another action like moving the object, selecting something else, or clicking away, the panel disappears and the opportunity to set initial parameters is gone. Practically, this means you should check it right after creation. For a UV Sphere you can change segments and rings to reduce polygon count. For a Cylinder you can change vertices and radius. For example, if you add a UV Sphere and realize it’s too dense for a low-poly game, reduce segments to 16 and rings to 8 before dismissing the panel. A frequent error is ignoring the panel then trying to reconstruct the object at the right resolution — that wastes time. Closing takeaway: form the habit of adding a primitive and immediately glancing at the Adjust Last Operation panel; what parameter would you change first for a game asset? The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process Flow › Adjust Last Operation
Use the redo panel right after adding
The panel is temporary and controls parameters like segments, rings, vertices, radius and size.
Step-by-step
  1. Add a primitive with Shift+A or Add > Mesh.
  2. Immediately look for the Add ... panel in the bottom-left (Adjust Last Operation).
  3. Change segments, rings, vertices, radius, or other fields as needed.
  4. Click in the viewport or perform another action to finalize the values.
Example
Add a UV Sphere, set segments to 16 and rings to 8 to reduce polygon count for a low-poly game asset.
Common mistake
Waiting until after other edits to change resolution forces a rebuild or extra edits later.
Key Takeaway

Set mesh resolution during creation via the Adjust Last Operation panel to save time and control performance.

Visual cue

screens.title: Deleting objects — confirmation and safe habits
screens.subtitle: How to remove objects cleanly and avoid accidental loss

narration.text: Deleting objects is straightforward but requires care. To remove an object select it, press the Delete key or X, and then confirm the 'Erase Selected?' prompt by clicking Delete or pressing Enter. That confirmation is an important safety net in complex scenes. Always verify your selection before confirming, especially when multiple objects overlap, because accidental deletes can be time-consuming to recover from. One practical habit is to save before performing large deletions with Ctrl+S, creating a restore point in case you need to revert. Another useful tip is to hide objects using Collections or the Outliner's visibility toggle when you want to remove them from view without deleting them permanently. For example, if you're cleaning up a scene and are unsure whether a prop is needed, move it into a temporary collection and disable its visibility rather than deleting it outright. Closing question: when would toggling collection visibility be a better choice than deleting an object? Core Action › Delete objects
How to delete safely
Select, press Delete or X, then confirm the prompt. Use save and collections to guard against accidental loss.
Quick checklist
  • Confirm exactly which objects are selected.
  • Save (Ctrl+S) before major deletions.
  • Consider hiding into a collection instead of deleting if unsure.
Key Takeaway

Use confirmation and saving to prevent accidental loss, and prefer collection hiding when unsure.

Concrete scenario
Before deleting many props, create a 'Backup' collection and move items there. If you need them back, toggle visibility rather than recreate them.

screens.title: Undo and Redo — your safety net while modeling
screens.subtitle: Use Ctrl+Z and Shift+Ctrl+Z, and understand undo step settings

narration.text: Undo and Redo are essential for fearless experimentation. Use Ctrl+Z to step backwards through your recent actions and Shift+Ctrl+Z to redo actions you just undid. Blender stores a history of actions and you can configure how many Undo steps are preserved in Edit > Preferences > System > Undo Steps. Increasing this value allows you to go further back in your workflow but uses more memory. A practical example is moving a sphere, scaling it, and realizing the scale was wrong — pressing Ctrl+Z repeatedly returns you through the history to the point before the scale. A common misconception is relying solely on Undo for safety instead of saving; always save before big changes because Undo history may be lost if the file is closed or if system limits are reached. Closing question: how would you balance undo depth and memory usage for a long modeling session on a modest machine? The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition › Undo & Redo
Undo and Redo basics
Ctrl+Z steps backwards. Shift+Ctrl+Z redoes. Configure Undo Steps in preferences to control history depth.
Practical example
Move, rotate and scale an object. If a step is wrong, press Ctrl+Z once or multiple times to return to the desired state, then use Shift+Ctrl+Z to move forward again if needed.
Preferences
Edit > Preferences > System > Undo Steps controls how far back you can go.
Common mistake
Relying on Undo instead of saving. If the file closes or undo history is cleared, you may lose undo states.
Key Takeaway

Combine Undo/Redo with frequent saves to experiment safely and avoid losing work.

Check your understanding
If you need to undo many steps but have limited memory, what trade-offs would you consider?
Concrete scenario
Set Undo Steps higher while doing detailed sculpting, then lower it again for memory-heavy rendering sessions if needed.

screens.title: Collections and the Outliner — organize your scene
screens.subtitle: Create collections, move objects with M, and use visibility and render toggles

narration.text: Collections are Blender's way of grouping objects for organization and control. They appear in the Outliner where you can create named collections such as Ground, Props, and Lights. To create a collection right-click in the Outliner and choose New Collection. To move objects into a collection, select them and press M, then pick an existing collection or create a new one. Collections let you hide, show, or disable rendering for all objects they contain, which is essential when working on large scenes or collaborating with a team. For example, place all environment props into an 'Environment_Props' collection; toggle its visibility to speed viewport performance while working on characters. A common misconception is thinking collections are only visual; they also affect render and selection behavior. Closing takeaway: start grouping objects into meaningful collections early so that your scene remains manageable as it grows. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process Flow › Collections
Why collections matter
They group objects for visibility, selection, and render control to manage complex scenes efficiently.
How to create and move
  1. Right-click in the Outliner and choose New Collection.
  2. Select objects in the viewport, press M, and choose a collection or create a new one.
  3. Use the checkbox and camera icon in the Outliner to hide or disable rendering for that collection.
Key Takeaway

Organize early with clear collection names to simplify hiding, rendering, and collaboration.

Concrete example
Create 'Ground' and 'Props' collections, move the plane to Ground and primitives to Props, then toggle Props to focus on terrain without clutter.
Common misconception
Collections are not just visual layers; they also control render and selection behavior for grouped objects.

screens.title: Practice: Populate and organize a simple scene
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step walkthrough of the chapter's hands-on activity

narration.text: Now we’ll walk through the hands-on activity that ties these skills together. Start by opening Blender and deleting the default cube with X then Delete. Next, add a UV Sphere with Shift+A > Mesh > UV Sphere, and immediately check the Add UV Sphere panel; set segments to 16 and rings to 8 so the sphere is low-poly for a game asset. Then add a Cylinder and in the Add Cylinder panel set vertices to 12 and radius to 0.5 so it sits proportionally beside the sphere. Add a Plane for the ground and scale it up significantly (S then 10 then Enter) so the sphere and cylinder can sit on it. Position the sphere and cylinder so they rest on the plane using G then Z to raise them. Practice Undo by moving the sphere and pressing Ctrl+Z to step back, then Shift+Ctrl+Z to redo. Finally create two collections in the Outliner: 'Ground' and 'Props', move the Plane into Ground using M, then select both sphere and cylinder and press M to move them into Props. Toggle visibility and rendering in the Outliner to confirm the organization. This sequence reinforces adding, immediate adjustment, deletion, undo, and scene organization in one flow.

keyIdea.title: Practice flow
keyIdea.text: Follow a sequence: delete defaults, add primitives, adjust parameters, position, undo/redo, then group into collections.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity › Populate & Organize
Step-by-step walkthrough
Follow these steps in Blender to practice all chapter skills in one short flow.
  1. Delete the default cube: select it, press X, then Delete to confirm.
  2. Add a UV Sphere: Shift+A > Mesh > UV Sphere. In the Add panel set Segments = 16, Rings = 8.
  3. Add a Cylinder: Shift+A > Mesh > Cylinder. Set Vertices = 12 and Radius = 0.5 in the Add panel.
  4. Add a Plane: Shift+A > Mesh > Plane. Select it and press S then 10 then Enter to scale.
  5. Position objects: select sphere, press G then Z and move it to sit on the plane; repeat for cylinder.
  6. Practice Undo/Redo: move the sphere, then press Ctrl+Z to undo and Shift+Ctrl+Z to redo.
  7. Create collections: in the Outliner, right-click and choose New Collection. Name one 'Ground' and one 'Props'.
  8. Move objects into collections: select the Plane, press M and choose 'Ground'; select sphere and cylinder, press M and choose 'Props'.
Key Takeaway

This flow ties adding, adjusting, deleting, undoing, and organizing into a repeatable practice for efficient modeling.

Quick tips
  • Always inspect the Add panel before performing another action.
  • Use collections to hide groups while you focus on others.
  • Save before big deletions to create a fallback.
Reflection
Which step saved you the most time: adjusting parameters immediately, or grouping into collections? Try both and compare.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Concise definitions and the most important takeaways

narration.text: Let's summarize the core concepts you should carry forward. First: primitives are basic geometric building blocks like cubes and spheres used to block out forms. narration.text: Finish with the tools and habits that keep your workflow reliable. First: always inspect the Adjust Last Operation panel immediately after adding a primitive to set segments, rings, and vertices to appropriate values. Second: use Delete or X with the confirmation prompt and save before major removals so you can recover if needed. Third: organize objects into Collections via the Outliner and use M to move items into collections; this enables hiding or disabling entire groups during focused work. These tools reduce wasted effort and help you maintain performance and clarity in your scenes. As a habit, adjust early, save often, and group objects — this combination will make modeling faster and safer.
